| fam11 = [[Franco-Provençal|Arpitan]]–[[Langues d'oïl|Oïl]] | fam12 = [[Langues d'oïl|Oïl]] | ancestor = [[Old Latin]] | ancestor2 = [[Vulgar Latin]] | ancestor3 = [[Proto-Romance language|Proto-Romance]] | ancestor4 = [[Gallo-Romance languages|Old Gallo-Romance]] | ancestor5 = [[Old French]] |iso3=zrp |linglist=zrp.html |glotto=zarp1238 |glottorefname=Zarphatic }} '''Zarphatic''', also called '''Judeo-French''' ({{langx|zrp|צרפתית}} {{translit|zrp|Tzarfatit}}) or '''Western Loez''',{{Cite book |last=Edzard |first=Alexandra B. |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/j.ctv2h439g6 |title=Jewish Languages: Text specimens, grammatical, lexical, and cultural sketches |date=2021 |publisher=Harrassowitz Verlag |isbn=978-3-447-11708-1 |pages=557, 561–75 |language=en |chapter=Judeo-French|jstor=j.ctv2h439g6 }} is a language that was spoken by the [[French Jews]] of northern [[France]] and in parts of western [[Germany]], such as [[Mainz]], [[Frankfurt am Main]] and [[Aix-la-Chapelle]]. It was also spoken by French Jews who moved to [[Norman England]].{{sfn|Hillaby|2013|pp=1, 112, 194-195}} Some have conjectured that the language influenced the development of [[Yiddish language|Yiddish]].{{cite encyclopedia|url=https://www.jewishvirtuallibrary.org/yiddish-language|title=Yiddish Language|last=Katznelson|first=Itzhak|encyclopedia=[[Encyclopedia Judaica]]|date=2008|authorlink=Itzhak Katzenelson|via=[[Jewish Virtual Library]]}}{{cite journal |last=Weinreich |first=M. |year=1959 |title=History of the Yiddish Language: The Problems and Their Implications |journal=Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society |volume=103 |issue=4 |pages=563–570 |jstor=985559}} == Etymology == The term ''Zarphatic'', coined by [[Solomon Birnbaum]],{{cite book |first=S. A. |last=Birnbaum |title=Yiddish: A Survey and a Grammar |edition=2nd |publisher=University of Toronto Press |year=2016 |page=33}} comes from the [[Hebrew]] name for France, {{Transliteration|he|[[Tzarfat]]}} ({{lang|he|צרפת}}), which was originally used in the [[Hebrew Bible]] as a name for the city of [[Sarepta]], in [[Phoenicia]]. Unlike most other [[Jewish languages]] which had many loan words from [[Hebrew]], it had relatively few. This has led to the conclusion that it may not have been a far-distant language but, instead, a dialect of [[Old French]].{{cn|date=October 2025}} ==History and use== Zarphatic was written using a variation of the [[Hebrew alphabet]]. It first appeared in this form in the 11th century in [[Gloss (annotation)|glosses]] of the [[Torah]] and [[Talmud]] written by the rabbis [[Moshe HaDarshan]] and [[Rashi]]. The language became secularised during the 13th century, becoming used in varied domains such as poetry, medicine, astronomy, and commerce. Most linguists agree that Zarphatic was not fundamentally different from [[Old French]], and that it was more of a writing system and literary tradition that reflected the Jewish culture of the day. According to some researchers,M. Weinreich et S. A. Birnbaum, cited by Marc Kiwitt, cf sources{{fcn|date=October 2025}} it was different from the Christian majority dialect, and thus a specific [[Judeo-Romance]] language. However, other linguists contend that it was essentially the same as Christian dialects of the same regions, with only some Hebrew influences.{{Cite web |title=Judeo-French |url=https://www.jewishlanguages.org/judeo-french |access-date=23 September 2024 |website=Jewish Languages |language=en |first1=Marc |last1=Kiwitt |first2=Julia |last2=Zwink}} It seems that Zarphatic was probably never a [[vernacular language]], and that the Jews of the area did not speak a differing language or dialect, at least not one distinguished by [[phonology]] or [[lexicon]] beyond that specific to a community.Jean Baumgarten in ''La question du judéo-français vue par les philologues allemands et français'', citing M. Bannitt; cf bibliographie{{fcn|date=October 2025}} Rather, it acted more as a liturgical language, for exegesis and literature. Its primary use was for explanation and [[vulgarisation]] of biblical and rabbinical literature. Most of the elements from the Hebrew language are found in the function words (articles, prepositions, etc.), though there are some changes to verbs and vocabulary.{{Cite book |last=Edzard |first=Alexandra B. |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/j.ctv2h439g6 |title=Jewish Languages: Text specimens, grammatical, lexical, and cultural sketches |date=2021 |publisher=Harrassowitz Verlag |isbn=978-3-447-11708-1 |pages=579, 585–589 |jstor=j.ctv2h439g6 |language=en}} === Extinction === Due to the constant persecution, killing and [[History of the Jews in France#Expulsions and Returns|expulsion of Jews from France]]{{cite web |url=https://history.com/this-day-in-history/king-charles-vi-of-france-orders-all-jews-expelled |website=History.com |title=King Charles VI of France orders all Jews expelled from the kingdom |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240605192427/https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/king-charles-vi-of-france-orders-all-jews-expelled |archive-date=5 June 2024}} and [[History of European Jews in the Middle Ages|other European nations]], the Zarphatic language likely went extinct in the 14th century; documentation of the language slows in the mid-14th century. The last known example of Zarphatic is a recipe for ''[[charoset]]'' written in 1470.{{Contradictory inline|reason=1470 is in the 15th century|date=May 2026}} == Writing system == Zarphatic was written using the Hebrew writing system and the [[Tiberian vocalization|Tiberian system]] for [[diacritic]]al markers and reflected some Latin writing traditions that help to distinguish it from a solely phonetic reproduction of spoken language. Not all Hebrew graphemes are used in Zarphatic: the graphemes [[kaph]] (כ), [[samekh]] (ס), and [[Taw|tav]] (ת), are rare, and [[Heth|ḥet]] (ח) and [[Ayin|ʕayin]] (ע) are omitted entirely. {| class="wikitable" |+Sample text !Language !Example text |- |Old French
